claim: Disc1-mutant mice show reduced average firing rates of fast-spiking interneurons in the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Single-unit recordings in awake mice revealed reduced average firing rates of fast-spiking interneurons (INTs), including optogenetically identified parvalbumin-positive cells
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental data from single-unit recordings in awake mice, as shown in Figure 1c (U = 43, p=0.017, Mann-Whitney U-test).

claim: Optogenetically identified parvalbumin-positive interneurons show reduced firing rates in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Single-unit recordings in awake mice revealed reduced average firing rates of fast-spiking interneurons (INTs), including optogenetically identified parvalbumin-positive cells
evidence: Supported by optogenetic identification experiments showing reduced spontaneous spiking of PVIs in Disc1-mutant mice (U = 47, p=0.029, Mann-Whitney U-test, Figure 1g).

claim: The proportion of interneurons phase-coupled to ongoing gamma oscillations is lower in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Single-unit recordings in awake mice revealed reduced average firing rates of fast-spiking interneurons (INTs), including optogenetically identified parvalbumin-positive cells, and a lower proportion of INTs phase-coupled to ongoing gamma oscillations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced proportion of INTs significantly phase-coupled to high-gamma oscillations from 73% in control to 39% in Disc1-mutant mice (t = −2.466, p=0.03, Figure 4c).

claim: Spike transmission efficacy at local pyramidal cell-interneuron connections is decreased in Disc1-mutant mice in vivo.
source: Moreover, we observed decreased spike transmission efficacy at local pyramidal cell (PYR)-INT connections in vivo, suggesting a reduced excitatory effect of local glutamatergic inputs as a potential mechanism of lower INT rates.
evidence: Supported by cross-correlation analysis showing spike transmission reduced to ~51% of control levels (t = 4.716, p=0.002, Figure 2d) and to ~42% at PYR-PVI connections (t = 2.653, p=0.029, Figure 2e).

claim: Reduced excitatory effect of local glutamatergic inputs is a potential mechanism of lower interneuron firing rates in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Moreover, we observed decreased spike transmission efficacy at local pyramidal cell (PYR)-INT connections in vivo, suggesting a reduced excitatory effect of local glutamatergic inputs as a potential mechanism of lower INT rates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between reduced spike transmission and lower INT firing rates.

claim: Assembly activations defined as coactivations within 25 ms occur equally often in Disc1-mutant and control mice.
source: While assembly activations defined as coactivations within 25 ms were observed equally often, the expression strength of individual assembly patterns was significantly higher in Disc1-mutant mice.
evidence: Supported by data showing comparable assembly activation rates between genotypes (t = −0.595, p=0.565, Figure 5d).

claim: The expression strength of individual assembly patterns is significantly higher in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: While assembly activations defined as coactivations within 25 ms were observed equally often, the expression strength of individual assembly patterns was significantly higher in Disc1-mutant mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing significantly larger assembly activation strength in Disc1-mutant mice (U = 4, p=0.026, Figure 5e).

claim: Disc1 plays a role in shaping the properties of prefrontal assembly patterns by setting interneuron responsiveness to glutamatergic drive.
source: Our data, thus, reveal a role of Disc1 in shaping the properties of prefrontal assembly patterns by setting INT responsiveness to glutamatergic drive.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined observations of reduced INT responsiveness and altered assembly patterns in Disc1-mutant mice.

claim: Cognitive impairment is a major burden for individuals suffering from psychiatric disease.
source: Cognitive impairment is a major burden for individuals suffering from psychiatric disease.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in the field of psychiatry.

claim: GABAergic interneurons play a critical role in the emergence of cognitive dysfunction in psychiatric illnesses.
source: A series of investigations has put emphasis on the critical role of GABAergic interneurons (INTs) in the emergence of cognitive dysfunction in psychiatric illnesses (Akbarian et al., 1995; Mirnics et al., 2000; Volk et al., 2000; Lewis et al., 2005; Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010; Lisman, 2012; Volk et al., 2016; Ferguson and Gao, 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive interneurons have attracted substantial attention among neocortical interneuron types.
source: Among the various neocortical INT types, especially fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive interneurons (PVIs) have attracted substantial attention.
evidence: This is a general statement about the research field supported by the context of subsequent citations.

claim: Postmortem data indicated reduced numbers of PVIs in the prefrontal cortex of schizophrenia patients.
source: Postmortem data indicated reduced numbers of PVIs and diminished expression of the GABA-synthetizing enzyme GAD in PVIs of the prefrontal cortex of schizophrenia patients (Lewis et al., 2005; Volk et al., 2016; Marín, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to postmortem studies.

claim: Diminished expression of the GABA-synthetizing enzyme GAD in PVIs of the prefrontal cortex has been observed in schizophrenia patients.
source: Postmortem data indicated reduced numbers of PVIs and diminished expression of the GABA-synthetizing enzyme GAD in PVIs of the prefrontal cortex of schizophrenia patients (Lewis et al., 2005; Volk et al., 2016; Marín, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to postmortem studies.

claim: Eliminating prefrontal PVI output signaling induced working memory deficits in mice.
source: Furthermore, eliminating prefrontal PVI output signaling induced working memory deficits in mice, underscoring the central role of PVI activity in cognitive function (Murray et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental study.

claim: Disc1-mutant mice resemble an ultra-rare mutation with high penetrance for schizophrenia and major depressive disorder.
source: Transgenic disrupted-in-schizophrenia-1 (Disc1)-mutant mice, which resemble an ultra-rare mutation with high penetrance for schizophrenia and major depressive disorder (Blackwood et al., 2001), show cognitive deficits, thus rendering Disc1-mutant mice a prime candidate to investigate the circuit mechanisms of a psychiatric disease (Koike et al., 2006; Kvajo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to genetic study.

claim: Disc1-mutant mice show cognitive deficits.
source: Transgenic disrupted-in-schizophrenia-1 (Disc1)-mutant mice, which resemble an ultra-rare mutation with high penetrance for schizophrenia and major depressive disorder (Blackwood et al., 2001), show cognitive deficits, thus rendering Disc1-mutant mice a prime candidate to investigate the circuit mechanisms of a psychiatric disease (Koike et al., 2006; Kvajo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex is an important center for cognitive function.
source: Much research has focused on the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) as an important center for cognitive function (Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Sigurdsson et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2015; Sauer et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016b; Chini et al., 2020; Duvarci et al., 2018; Kaefer et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: In vitro studies in Disc1-mutants have put forward evidence for altered GABAergic signaling in the mPFC.
source: In vitro studies in Disc1-mutants have put forward evidence for altered GABAergic (Sauer et al., 2015) and glutamatergic signaling in the mPFC (Crabtree et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to in vitro study.

claim: In vitro studies in Disc1-mutants have put forward evidence for altered glutamatergic signaling in the mPFC.
source: In vitro studies in Disc1-mutants have put forward evidence for altered GABAergic (Sauer et al., 2015) and glutamatergic signaling in the mPFC (Crabtree et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to in vitro study.

claim: In mice haploinsufficient for DISC1 isoforms, prefrontal PVIs receive reduced excitatory drive from afferents originating in the medio-dorsal thalamus.
source: Moreover, in mice haploinsufficient for DISC1 isoforms (Seshadri et al., 2015), prefrontal PVIs receive reduced excitatory drive from afferents originating in the medio-dorsal thalamus (Delevich et al., 2020), a major input to the mPFC involved in cognitive function (Bolkan et al., 2017; Parnaudeau et al., 2013; Schmitt et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to electrophysiological study.

claim: The medio-dorsal thalamus is a major input to the mPFC involved in cognitive function.
source: Moreover, in mice haploinsufficient for DISC1 isoforms (Seshadri et al., 2015), prefrontal PVIs receive reduced excitatory drive from afferents originating in the medio-dorsal thalamus (Delevich et al., 2020), a major input to the mPFC involved in cognitive function (Bolkan et al., 2017; Parnaudeau et al., 2013; Schmitt et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Overexpressing Disc1 carrying a mutation previously associated with schizophrenia-related behavioral impairments selectively in cortical pyramidal cells results in decreased PV expression in PVIs.
source: In addition, overexpressing Disc1 carrying a mutation previously associated with schizophrenia-related behavioral impairments (Clapcote et al., 2007) selectively in cortical pyramidal cells (PYRs) results in decreased PV expression in PVIs, suggesting that impaired communication in local cortical circuits might contribute to Disc1-mediated INT dysfunction (Borkowska et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to genetic manipulation study.

claim: Impaired communication in local cortical circuits might contribute to Disc1-mediated interneuron dysfunction.
source: In addition, overexpressing Disc1 carrying a mutation previously associated with schizophrenia-related behavioral impairments (Clapcote et al., 2007) selectively in cortical pyramidal cells (PYRs) results in decreased PV expression in PVIs, suggesting that impaired communication in local cortical circuits might contribute to Disc1-mediated INT dysfunction (Borkowska et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cited experimental findings.

claim: Studies investigating the activity profile and local synaptic communication among prefrontal circuit components of Disc1-mutant mice in vivo are lacking.
source: However, studies investigating the activity profile and local synaptic communication among prefrontal circuit components of Disc1-mutant mice in vivo are lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: Mice carrying an N-terminal truncation in the DISC1 gene show reduced firing rates of PVIs in the nucleus accumbens in vivo.
source: Furthermore, previous work identified reduced firing rates of PVIs in the nucleus accumbens of mice carrying an N-terminal truncation in the DISC1 gene in vivo (Zhou et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to in vivo electrophysiology study.

claim: It is not known whether impairments of PVIs might contribute to altered network function in the mPFC of Disc1-mutant mice.
source: but whether impairments of PVIs might contribute to altered network function in the mPFC of Disc1-mutant mice is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Disc1-mutant mice have been shown to express impaired execution of working memory.
source: Disc1-mutant mice have been shown to express impaired execution of working memory (Koike et al., 2006; Kvajo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Single-unit recordings were performed from the mPFC of Disc1-mutant (n = 9) and control mice (n = 7) that were awake in their home cage.
source: To assess the potential network alterations underlying cognitive impairment, we performed single-unit recordings from the mPFC of Disc1-mutant (n = 9) and control mice (n = 7) that were awake in their home cage
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: 720 pyramidal cells were recorded in Disc1-mutant mice and 613 in control mice.
source: and analyzed discharge rates of PYRs (n = 720 and 613 in Disc1-mutant and control, respectively) and INTs (n = 104 and 79 in Disc1 and control, respectively; Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the sample sizes in the study.

claim: 104 interneurons were recorded in Disc1-mutant mice and 79 in control mice.
source: and analyzed discharge rates of PYRs (n = 720 and 613 in Disc1-mutant and control, respectively) and INTs (n = 104 and 79 in Disc1 and control, respectively; Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the sample sizes in the study.

claim: Neuron types were separated based on spike waveform kinetics.
source: Both neuron types were separated based on spike waveform kinetics (Sirota et al., 2008; Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the methodology for cell type classification, supported by citation.

claim: Firing rates of pyramidal cells were unaltered in Disc1-mutant mice compared to controls.
source: We found a significant reduction in INT firing rates in Disc1-mutant mice (U = 43, p=0.017, n = 7 mice each with electrophysiologically identified INTs, Mann–Whitney U-test), while the firing rates of PYRs were unaltered (t = 0.545, p=0.620, n = 9 Disc1-mutant and 7 control mice, unpaired t-test; Figure 1b and c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t = 0.545, p=0.620).

claim: Reduced firing rates of interneurons were preserved when analysis was based on INTs with low activity levels.
source: Reduced firing rates of INTs were preserved when we based the analysis on INTs with low activity levels (lowest third of the firing rate distribution, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by subsampling analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Unaltered PYR firing rates between genotypes were observed when only PYRs with high firing rate were considered.
source: Similarly, unaltered PYR firing rates between genotypes were observed when only PYRs with high firing rate were considered (highest third of the firing rate distribution, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by subsampling analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neocortical interneuron types are highly diverse.
source: Since neocortical INT types are highly diverse (Gupta et al., 2000; Druckmann et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to classification studies.

claim: Putative INTs identified by their spike shape might include a mixed set of GABAergic populations.
source: putative INTs identified by their spike shape might include a mixed set of GABAergic populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known diversity of interneuron types.

claim: ChR2 expression was highly specific for PVIs.
source: ChR2 expression was highly specific for PVIs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Spike waveform properties of PVIs clustered with electrophysiologically identified INTs.
source: Moreover, spike waveform properties of PVIs clustered with electrophysiologically identified INTs (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by waveform analysis shown in figures.

claim: Spike rates of light-sensitive cells increased rapidly upon laser onset.
source: and spike rates of light-sensitive cells increased rapidly upon laser onset (Figure 1—figure supplement 5)
evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The reduction in PVI activity in Disc1-mutant mice could not be explained by an altered speed modulation.
source: The reduction in PVI activity in Disc1-mutant mice could not be explained by an altered speed modulation because Disc1-mutant mice ran at comparable velocity as control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by behavioral analysis showing no difference in running speed (U = 4.0, p=0.298).

claim: Similar results of reduced PVI firing rates were obtained during recordings under ketamine anesthesia in a separate cohort of mice.
source: Furthermore, similar results of reduced PVI firing rates were obtained during recordings under ketamine anesthesia in a separate cohort of mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by anesthetized recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Loss of Disc1 expression results in impaired activity levels of interneurons, including PVIs.
source: Thus, loss of Disc1 expression results in impaired activity levels of INTs, including PVIs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental observations of reduced INT and PVI firing rates.

claim: PYR-INT connections can be captured by spike train cross-correlations in simultaneous recordings of large neuronal populations.
source: These connections can be captured by spike train cross-correlations in simultaneous recordings of large neuronal populations (English et al., 2017; Figure 2a–c).
evidence: Supported by citation to methodological study and demonstration in Figure 2.

claim: Among 7744 PYR-INT pairs tested, 135 significant monosynaptic interactions were detected.
source: Among 7744 PYR-INT pairs tested, we detected 135 significant monosynaptic interactions.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental results.

claim: The probability of finding PYR-INT connections was not different among genotypes.
source: The probability of finding PYR-INT connections was not different among genotypes (U = 36, p=0.158, n = 7 mice each, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of connection probability.

claim: Cross-correlation analysis revealed significantly reduced spike transmission to ~51% of control levels in the mPFC of Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Cross-correlation analysis revealed significantly reduced spike transmission to ~51% of control levels in the mPFC of Disc1-mutant mice (t = 4.716, p=0.002, n = 5 Disc1-mutant and 6 control mice, unpaired t-test; Figure 2c and d).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of spike transmission probability data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Spike transmission at connections to optogenetically identified PVIs was reduced to ~42% in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Furthermore, spike transmission at connections to optogenetically identified PVIs was reduced to ~42% (t = 2.653, p=0.029, Welch's test, n = 10 Disc1-mutant and 7 control connections, Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of PYR-PVI spike transmission data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The strength of spike transmission was inversely correlated with distance in both control and Disc1-mutant connections.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Zhou et al., 2021), the strength of the spike transmission was inversely correlated with distance in both control (Spearman's r = −0.336, p=0.018, n = 49 connections) and Disc1-mutant connections (Spearman's r = −0.345, p=0.024, n = 43 connections, Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3b and citation to previous work.

claim: Connected pairs in Disc1-mutant and control mice were similarly spaced.
source: Connected pairs in Disc1-mutant and control mice were similarly spaced (t = −0.458, p=0.648, n = 49 Disc1-mutant and 43 control connections, Welch's test, Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of intersomatic distances shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Multiple PYRs converge onto one INT with no significant difference in the number of presynaptic partners between genotypes.
source: We moreover consistently observed converging input of multiple (>1) PYRs onto one INT with no significant difference in the number of presynaptic partners between genotypes (U = 536, p=0.527, n = 39 Disc1-mutant and 34 control connections, Mann–Whitney U-test, Figure 3d, left).
evidence: Supported by analysis of convergence shown in Figure 3d.

claim: PYRs of both groups made frequent contact with more than one postsynaptic INT, with no significant difference in the number of divergent targets.
source: Similarly, PYRs of both groups made frequent contact with more than one postsynaptic INT, with no significant difference in the number of divergent targets (U = 595.5, p=0.204, n = 27 Disc1-mutant and 49 control connections, Mann–Whitney U-test, Figure 3d, right)
evidence: Supported by analysis of divergence shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Overall PYR-INT network structure is intact in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: indicating intact overall PYR-INT network structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations of similar convergence, divergence, and intersomatic distances.

claim: Synchronous presynaptic activity of PYRs with a common postsynaptic target has been demonstrated to boost spike transmission in the hippocampus.
source: Second, synchronous presynaptic activity of PYRs with a common postsynaptic target has been demonstrated to boost spike transmission in the hippocampus (English et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Excess synchronization of convergent PYRs in a 25 ms window was not significantly different between Disc1-mutant and control mice.
source: Excess synchronization of convergent PYRs in a 25 ms window was not significantly different between Disc1-mutant and control mice (t = 0.280, n = 121 and 55 PYR pairs, p=0.780, Welch's test, Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of presynaptic synchronization shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Defective synchronization of PYRs is ruled out as a mechanism of reduced spike transmission.
source: These findings rule out defective synchronization of PYRs as a mechanism of reduced spike transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding of similar presynaptic synchronization between genotypes.

claim: Hippocampal INTs show resonance membrane properties that boost spike transmission when postsynaptic spikes occur within an ~20–50 ms time interval.
source: Third, hippocampal INTs show resonance membrane properties that boost spike transmission when postsynaptic spikes occur within an ~20–50 ms time interval (English et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Neocortical PYR-INT connections displayed an approximately threefold boost of spike transmission probability in the resonance time window of 20–50 ms.
source: Consistent with reports from the hippocampus, neocortical PYR-INT connections displayed an approximately threefold boost of spike transmission probability in the resonance time window of 20–50 ms, similar to the gain observed in CA1 (English et al., 2017; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and comparison to cited study.

claim: Identified PVIs showed approximately twofold resonance boosting of spike transmission.
source: Moreover, identified PVIs showed approximately twofold resonance boosting of spike transmission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The magnitude of the resonance gain reached similar levels for PYR-INT pairs in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: However, the magnitude of the resonance gain reached similar levels for PYR-INT pairs in Disc1-mutant mice (t = 0.875, p=0.436, n = 53 Disc1-mutant and 71 control pairs, Welch's test, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Resonance boosting of spike transmission was significantly higher in identified PVIs in Disc1 compared to controls.
source: In identified PVIs, resonance boosting of spike transmission was even significantly higher in Disc1 compared to controls (U = 11, p=0.022, n = 10 Disc1-mutant and 6 control connections, Mann–Whitney U-test, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Reduced spike transmission in Disc1-mutant mice was evident when only considering spikes in the resonance time window.
source: Finally, reduced spike transmission in Disc1-mutant mice was also evident when we only considered spikes in the resonance time window (t = 4.530, p=0.0014, n = 5 Disc1-mutant and 6 control mice, unpaired t-test, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: INTs in the Disc1-mutant mPFC display intact convergence, responses to synchronous input and resonance properties.
source: Jointly, these data suggest that while INTs in the Disc1-mutant mPFC display intact convergence, responses to synchronous input and resonance properties, they respond less to the action of local glutamatergic synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the combined experimental observations.

claim: INTs in the Disc1-mutant mPFC respond less to the action of local glutamatergic synaptic transmission.
source: Jointly, these data suggest that while INTs in the Disc1-mutant mPFC display intact convergence, responses to synchronous input and resonance properties, they respond less to the action of local glutamatergic synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced spike transmission despite intact network properties.

claim: The timed activation of PVIs is a crucial determinant of the emergence and synchrony of gamma oscillations.
source: The timed activation of PVIs is a crucial determinant of the emergence and synchrony of gamma oscillations (Bartos et al., 2007; Sohal et al., 2009; Cardin et al., 2009; Perrenoud et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Power spectral density of local field potentials in the high-gamma frequency range (60–90 Hz) was significantly reduced to ~55% in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Power spectral density of local field potentials (LFPs) in the high-gamma frequency range (60–90 Hz) was significantly reduced to ~55% in Disc1-mutant mice (t = −2.728, p=0.016, n = 9 Disc1-mutant and 7 control mice, unpaired t-test, Figure 4a and b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Neither LFP power in the theta (6–12 Hz) nor low-gamma regime (20–40 Hz) were significantly affected in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: In contrast, neither LFP power in the theta (6–12 Hz, t = −0.15, p=0.883) nor low-gamma regime (20–40 Hz, t = −1.033, p=0.319) were significantly affected (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of LFP power shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The proportion of INTs that discharged significantly phase-coupled to high-gamma oscillations was reduced from 73% in control to 39% in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Moreover, the proportion of INTs that discharged significantly phase-coupled to high-gamma oscillations was reduced from 73% in control to 39% in Disc1-mutant mice (t = −2.466, p=0.03, n = 6 Disc1-mutant and 6 control mice, unpaired t-test, Figure 4c)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of phase-coupling shown in Figure 4c.

claim: No effect of genotype was observed for low-gamma oscillations on INT phase-coupling.
source: while no effect of genotype was observed for low-gamma oscillations (t = −0.897, p=0.393, n = 5 mice each, unpaired t-test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Preferred gamma phase and strength of gamma phase locking of significantly gamma-entrained INTs did not differ between genotypes.
source: Preferred gamma phase and strength of gamma phase locking of significantly gamma-entrained INTs did not differ between genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of significantly gamma-coupled PYRs was lower than that of INTs.
source: The proportion of significantly gamma-coupled PYRs was lower than that of INTs (~14% and ~25% in Disc1-mutant and control mice, respectively)
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental observations.

claim: The proportion of significantly gamma-coupled PYRs was not significantly different between genotypes.
source: and not significantly different between genotypes, irrespective of the gamma frequency band studied (low gamma: t = −2.62, p=0.8, n = 5 mice each; high gamma: t = −0.214, p=0.835, n = 5 Disc1-mutant and 6 control mice, unpaired t-tests; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: INT spiking occurs synchronized with gamma oscillations.
source: In agreement with previous work, these results suggest that INT spiking occurs synchronized with gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spike-triggered LFP analysis and comparison to previous work.

claim: The amplitude of INT spike-triggered high-gamma oscillations was significantly reduced in Disc1-mutant mice compared to controls.
source: The amplitude of INT spike-triggered high-gamma oscillations was significantly reduced in Disc1-mutant mice compared to controls (t = −3.431, p=0.011, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey tests, Figure 4d and e).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Spike-triggered gamma amplitudes significantly exceeded random-triggered amplitudes in control mice.
source: Moreover, while spike-triggered gamma amplitudes significantly exceeded random-triggered amplitudes in control mice (t = 4.537, p=0.001), this effect was strongly reduced in Disc1-mutant mice and did not reach significance (t = 1.268, p=0.591, Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Restricting analysis to INT spikes that followed spiking in a presynaptic PYR within 2 ms revealed no difference in the amplitude of spike-triggered gamma oscillations between genotypes.
source: Notably, restricting the analysis to INT spikes that followed spiking in a presynaptic PYR within 2 ms (i.e., likely reflecting activation of the INT by local PYRs) revealed no difference in the amplitude of spike-triggered gamma oscillations between genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Impaired gamma oscillations are not a simple reflection of defective excitatory drive in local PYR-INT loops.
source: These results suggest that impaired gamma oscillations are not a simple reflection of defective excitatory drive in local PYR-INT loops.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that spike-triggered gamma is normal when restricted to synaptically-driven INT spikes.

claim: Reduced zero time-lag synchrony of pairs of simultaneously recorded INTs was found in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Consistent with the impaired high-gamma synchronization of INTs, we found reduced zero time-lag synchrony of pairs of simultaneously recorded INTs in Disc1-mutant mice (U = 42, p=0.026, n = 7 mice each, Mann–Whitney U-test, Figure 4f and g).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Disc1-mutant mice demonstrate impaired high-gamma oscillations and a decoupling of INTs from fast network oscillations.
source: These results jointly demonstrate impaired high-gamma oscillations and a decoupling of INTs from fast network oscillations in Disc1-mutant mice.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the combined observations of reduced gamma power, reduced INT phase-coupling, and reduced INT synchrony.

claim: An important function of GABAergic inhibition might be to decorrelate synchronous activity of pyramidal cells imposed by shared inputs.
source: Previous experimental and simulation studies suggested that an important function of GABAergic inhibition might be to decorrelate synchronous activity of pyramidal cells imposed by shared inputs (Renart et al., 2010; Tetzlaff et al., 2012; Sippy and Yuste, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous experimental and theoretical studies.

claim: Feedback inhibition within a circuit is particularly effective at constraining pairwise spike train correlations.
source: Theoretical work further emphasized that feedback inhibition within a circuit is particularly effective at constraining pairwise spike train correlations (Tetzlaff et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical study.

claim: PYRs in the Disc1 mPFC displayed stronger pairwise synchronization at 25 ms time scale at the level of individual neuron pairs.
source: In the Disc1 mPFC, PYRs indeed displayed stronger pairwise synchronization at 25 ms time scale at the level of individual neuron pairs (t = −9.437, p=6.5 * 10–21, n = 1797 control and 2445 Disc1 PYR pairs, this analysis considered all PYRs, Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: No significant difference in pairwise PYR synchronization was found at the level of mouse averages.
source: However, this analysis revealed no significant difference in the level of mouse averages (t = −0.178, p=0.861, n = 7 control and 9 Disc1-mutant mice, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis at the mouse level.

claim: Groups of coactive cells forming neuronal assemblies are thought to be a hallmark of cortical processing.
source: Groups of coactive cells forming neuronal assemblies are thought to be a hallmark of cortical processing (Buzsáki, 2010; El-Gaby et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: 113 assembly patterns were detected in control mice and 122 patterns in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Using this procedure, we detected in total 113 assembly patterns in control mice (n = 6) and 122 patterns in Disc1-mutant mice (n = 6)
evidence: This is a direct report of the assembly detection results.

claim: One assembly pattern was found per 5.3 ± 0.6 PYRs in control mice and 5.1 ± 0.8 PYRs in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: with one assembly pattern found per 5.3 ± 0.6 and 5.1 ± 0.8 PYRs in control and Disc1 mPFC, respectively (U = 19, p=0.936, n = 6 mice each, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of assembly density.

claim: Neurons with large weight in a detected assembly pattern showed more pronounced co-firing than neurons that contributed less to a given pattern.
source: Neurons with large weight in a detected assembly pattern showed more pronounced co-firing than neurons that contributed less to a given pattern (Figure 5c), corroborating the validity of the assembly detection method.
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5c, which validates the assembly detection method.

claim: Spontaneous assembly patterns activated at comparable rates in control and Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Spontaneous assembly patterns activated at comparable rates in control and Disc1-mutant mice (t = −0.595, p=0.565, six mice each, unpaired t-test, Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The assembly activation strength was significantly larger in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: However, consistent with enhanced pairwise co-firing detected on the level of individual cells, the assembly activation strength was significantly larger in Disc1-mutant mice (U = 4, p=0.026, n = 6 mice each, Mann–Whitney U-test, Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Altered assembly structure exists in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: These data jointly indicate altered assembly structure in Disc1-mutant mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased assembly activation strength.

claim: Fast-spiking INTs show task-dependent tuning during working memory.
source: Despite the broad recognition that fast-spiking INTs, particularly PVIs, contribute to neuronal network synchronization at gamma frequencies (Bartos et al., 2007; Sohal et al., 2009; Cardin et al., 2009), show task-dependent tuning during working memory (Kim et al., 2016b; Lagler et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fast-spiking INTs are required for the proper execution of working memory.
source: and are required for the proper execution of working memory (Murray et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Information is lacking on PVIs' activity in the prefrontal cortex of working memory-deficient Disc1-mutant mice.
source: information is still lacking on PVIs' activity in the prefrontal cortex of working memory-deficient Disc1-mutant mice.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The average discharge rates of INTs are reduced in vivo by ~44% in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Extending upon previous electrophysiological Disc1 studies (Sauer et al., 2015; Chini et al., 2020; Delevich et al., 2020; Kaefer et al., 2019), we show that the average discharge rates of INTs are reduced in vivo by ~44%, whereas PYR activity is unaltered (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: An ~41% reduction in the magnitude of spike transmission probability at PYR-PVI connections was detected in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Related to the reduced mean PVI activity, we detected an ~41% reduction in the magnitude of spike transmission probability at PYR-PVI connections with unaltered probability of finding connected PYR-INT pairs in Disc1-mutant mice (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d and e.

claim: The probability of finding connected PYR-INT pairs is unaltered in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Related to the reduced mean PVI activity, we detected an ~41% reduction in the magnitude of spike transmission probability at PYR-PVI connections with unaltered probability of finding connected PYR-INT pairs in Disc1-mutant mice (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data.

claim: A limitation of the study is the comparably low number of optogenetically identified PVIs.
source: Although the firing rates and spike waveform properties of PVIs were indistinguishable from electrophysiologically identified putative fast-spiking INTs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), it should be noted that a limitation of our study is the comparable low number of optogenetically identified PVIs.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: Spike transmission is an indirect estimation of synaptic connections onto INTs.
source: Spike transmission is an indirect estimation of synaptic connections onto INTs (English et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to methodological study.

claim: The weaker spike transmission is unlikely to be caused by network effects such as altered convergence or intersomatic distance between the connected cells.
source: Control analyses demonstrated that the weaker spike transmission is unlikely to be caused by network effects such as altered convergence or intersomatic distance between the connected cells, suggesting that it reflects a genuine reduction in excitatory drive at PYR-INT connections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the control analyses showing intact network properties.

claim: The weaker spike transmission reflects a genuine reduction in excitatory drive at PYR-INT connections.
source: Control analyses demonstrated that the weaker spike transmission is unlikely to be caused by network effects such as altered convergence or intersomatic distance between the connected cells, suggesting that it reflects a genuine reduction in excitatory drive at PYR-INT connections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the exclusion of alternative explanations.

claim: It is likely that the number of detected pairs might have been undersampled in Disc1-mutant mice given the lower spike transmission probability.
source: Given the lower spike transmission probability in Disc1-mutant mice, it is, however, likely that the number of detected pairs might have been undersampled in Disc1-mutant mice.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential methodological limitation.

claim: Reduced numbers of excitatory connections from local PYRs onto INTs might compose one contributing factor to reduced spike transmission.
source: Reduced numbers of excitatory connections from local PYRs onto INTs might compose one contributing factor.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: Disc1-mutant mice show altered wiring of excitatory connections in the hippocampal dentate gyrus-to-CA3 pathway.
source: Indeed, Disc1-mutant mice show altered wiring of excitatory connections in the hippocampal dentate gyrus-to-CA3 pathway (Kvajo et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Analysis of the mPFC revealed no apparent changes in excitatory axon distribution in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: although analysis of the mPFC revealed no apparent changes in excitatory axon distribution (Crabtree et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Insufficient expression of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) in cortical INTs might be a potential factor contributing to reduced spike transmission.
source: Another potential factor might be the insufficient expression of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) in cortical INTs.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: Removing NMDARs specifically from cortical PVIs induces working memory and prepulse inhibition impairments in mice.
source: Removing NMDARs specifically from cortical PVIs induces working memory and prepulse inhibition impairments in mice, reminiscent of symptoms observed in schizophrenia patients (Belforte et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The observed lower spike transmission probability might be caused by reduced excitability of INTs in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Furthermore, it is possible that the observed lower spike transmission probability is caused by reduced excitability of INTs in Disc1-mutant mice.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: Blocking T-type calcium channels in PVIs results in reduced numbers of cfos-positive PVIs in a social interaction task.
source: For instance, blocking T-type calcium channels in PVIs results in reduced numbers of cfos-positive PVIs in a social interaction task (Shen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Reduced expression of T-type channels has been reported in mice upon PVI-specific deletion of the schizophrenia-associated gene FXR1.
source: Notably, reduced expression of T-type channels has been reported in mice upon PVI-specific deletion of the schizophrenia-associated gene FXR1 (FMR1 autosome homolog 1), although potential defects in T-type channel expression specifically in Disc1-mutant mice are unclear (Shen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Whole-cell recordings from PVIs in prefrontal slices of Disc1-mutant mice failed to detect changes in intrinsic excitability in vitro.
source: Although whole-cell recordings from PVIs in prefrontal slices of Disc1-mutant mice failed to detect changes in intrinsic excitability in vitro (Delevich et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: It cannot be ruled out that differences in PVI excitability might exist in the intact circuitry under conditions of physiological neuromodulatory inputs.
source: it cannot be ruled out that such differences might exist in the intact circuitry under conditions of physiological neuromodulatory inputs.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential differences between in vitro and in vivo conditions.

claim: PVIs in slice preparations of mice expressing dominant-negative DISC1 show reduced current injection-induced firing rate increases in response to bath application of dopamine 2 receptor agonists.
source: This is particularly relevant because PVIs in slice preparations of mice expressing dominant-negative DISC1 (Hikida et al., 2007) show reduced current injection-induced firing rate increases in response to bath application of dopamine 2 receptor agonists (Cardarelli et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Diminished recruitment of PVIs by local glutamatergic inputs will result in lower PVI firing rates and weaker PVI-mediated synaptic inhibition.
source: On the level of neuronal networks, we propose that reduced drive to INTs induces a chain of interrelated functional consequences. Diminished recruitment of PVIs by local glutamatergic inputs will result in lower PVI firing rates and weaker PVI-mediated synaptic inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference about the network-level consequences of reduced INT drive.

claim: Lower synchrony of PVIs might result in the observed reduction in gamma power in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Lower synchrony of PVIs might consequently result in the observed reduction in gamma power in Disc1-mutant mice (Kim et al., 2016a; Wang and Carlén, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous studies on PVI-gamma relationships.

claim: A gamma oscillation dysfunction in the mPFC might contribute to working memory deficits in Disc1-mutants.
source: Moreover, a gamma oscillation dysfunction in the mPFC might contribute to working memory deficits in Disc1-mutants.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional consequences of gamma dysfunction.

claim: High-gamma activities occur during the execution of working memory in mice and monkeys.
source: This proposal fits to reports of high-gamma activities occurring during the execution of working memory in mice (Yamamoto et al., 2014) and monkeys (Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reduced PVI activity and consequently reduced perisomatic inhibition might be expected to lead to enhanced PYR discharge rates.
source: One might expect that reduced PVI activity and consequently reduced perisomatic inhibition (Courtin et al., 2014) may lead to enhanced PYR discharge rates.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known role of perisomatic inhibition.

claim: No significant changes in the average activity or gamma phase relationship of PYRs were observed in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: However, we did not observe significant changes in the average activity or gamma phase relationship of PYRs.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental observations.

claim: The compound inhibitory conductance emerging from the convergence of active GABAergic perisomatic inputs onto a single PYR might be sufficiently large to control the activity of PYR populations.
source: Since perisomatic inhibition generates large GABAA receptor-mediated conductances at unitary GABAergic connections (Jouhanneau et al., 2018), the compound inhibitory conductance emerging from the convergence of active GABAergic perisomatic inputs onto a single PYR might be sufficiently large to control the activity of PYR populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of perisomatic inhibition and citation to previous work.

claim: Pharmacogenetic silencing of hippocampal PVIs or the elimination of PVI synaptic output with tetanus toxin had no effect on the expression of the activity marker cfos.
source: This hypothesis fits to previous studies showing that pharmacogenetic silencing of hippocampal PVIs or the elimination of PVI synaptic output with tetanus toxin had no effect on the expression of the activity marker cfos (Murray et al., 2011; Stefanelli et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is conceivable that synaptic connections among local PYRs might be reduced in their efficacy in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Additional factors might contribute to preserved PYR firing rates. It is conceivable that synaptic connections among local PYRs might be reduced in their efficacy.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: Due to the small amplitude of excitatory postsynaptic potentials at PYR-PYR connections it is challenging to detect them in vivo for the quantification of spike transmission probability.
source: However, due to the small amplitude of excitatory postsynaptic potentials at PYR-PYR connections it is challenging to detect them in vivo for the quantification of spike transmission probability (Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about a methodological limitation supported by citation.

claim: It remains unclear whether firing rates of other neocortical interneuron types such as somatostatin-positive INTs are altered in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Moreover, it remains unclear whether firing rates of other neocortical interneuron types such as somatostatin-positive INTs are altered in Disc1-mutant mice.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in knowledge.

claim: Somatostatin-positive INTs efficiently control activity levels of local principal cells in the hippocampus.
source: Quantifications of cfos expression levels revealed that somatostatin-positive INTs efficiently control activity levels of local principal cells in the hippocampus (Stefanelli et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Enhanced inhibitory tone provided by somatostatin-positive INTs might counteract the reduced inhibitory inputs from PVIs.
source: Enhanced inhibitory tone provided by these INTs might, thus, counteract the reduced inhibitory inputs from PVIs.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential compensatory mechanism.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of PVIs enhanced pairwise correlations among cortical PYRs.
source: In line with this hypothesis, chemogenetic silencing of PVIs enhanced pairwise correlations among cortical PYRs (Hamm et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The expression strength of neuronal assemblies reflects the number of coactive cells, their synchronization and firing rate.
source: The expression strength of neuronal assemblies as evaluated with the method chosen here reflects the number of coactive cells, their synchronization and firing rate.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of the assembly analysis method.

claim: A time window of 25 ms was chosen to detect assembly patterns, which is within the integration time of cortical PYRs.
source: Importantly, we chose a time window of 25 ms to detect assembly patterns, which is within the integration time of cortical PYRs (Koch et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on neuronal integration time.

claim: Active assemblies within the 25 ms integration window are expected to efficiently affect downstream reader neurons.
source: Active assemblies within this integration window are, thus, expected to efficiently affect downstream reader neurons (Buzsáki, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known integration time of neurons and citation to theoretical work.

claim: Disturbed cell assembly expressions have been identified in the chronic ketamine and Df(16)A+/- models of schizophrenia.
source: Disturbed cell assembly expressions have been identified in the chronic ketamine and Df(16 )A+/- models of schizophrenia (Hamm et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In the chronic ketamine and Df(16)A+/- models, stability of assembly patterns rather than their expression strength were affected.
source: Notably, in those models, stability of assembly patterns rather than their expression strength were affected.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from previous studies.

claim: While the nature of the assembly dysfunction might differ between distinct models, altered assembly expressions might be a common final path underlying cognitive disturbances in schizophrenia.
source: These data imply that while the nature of the assembly dysfunction might differ between distinct models, altered assembly expressions might be a common final path underlying cognitive disturbances in schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a speculation about a general principle across different models.

claim: Enhanced activation strength means that neurons that are part of an assembly tend to co-fire more strongly in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: What are the potential functional implications of increased assembly activation strength for cognition? Enhanced activation strength means that neurons that are part of an assembly tend to co-fire more strongly in Disc1-mutant mice.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the assembly activation strength measure.

claim: Recurrent excitatory connections and Hebbian plasticity among PYRs are thought to underlie the formation and maintenance of cell assemblies.
source: Recurrent excitatory connections and Hebbian plasticity among PYRs are thought to underlie the formation and maintenance of cell assemblies (Harris, 2005; Palm et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Previous work identified increased synaptic plasticity at layer 2/3-to-layer 5 glutamatergic synapses of Disc1-mutant mice.
source: Previous work identified increased synaptic plasticity at layer 2/3-to-layer 5 glutamatergic synapses of Disc1-mutant mice (Crabtree et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Increased synaptic plasticity might support the emergence of stronger assemblies in addition to reduced inhibitory input.
source: which might support the emergence of stronger assemblies in addition to reduced inhibitory input.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: Cell assemblies in the mPFC of Disc1-mutant mice might retain larger stability over time given the stronger reactivation.
source: Given the stronger reactivation of cell assemblies in the mPFC of Disc1-mutant mice, we propose they might retain larger stability over time.
evidence: This is a speculation about the temporal dynamics of assemblies.

claim: Both stable and transiently active assemblies have been identified in the visual cortex using in vivo calcium imaging methods.
source: In the visual cortex, both stable (i.e., repeatedly active over weeks) and transiently active (i.e., largely restricted to one experimental session) assemblies have been identified using in vivo calcium imaging methods (Pérez-Ortega et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Stable cell assemblies might relate to representations of long-term memories, while transient cell assemblies could reflect the emergence of new assemblies.
source: It has been previously suggested that stable cell assemblies might relate to representations of long-term memories, while transient cell assemblies could reflect the emergence of new assemblies (Pérez-Ortega et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: There is a trade-off between stable representations and dynamic encoding of memory content.
source: This conjecture proposes a trade-off between stable representations and dynamic encoding of memory content.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposition based on the cited work.

claim: This trade-off might be shifted toward the stable side in Disc1-mutant mice.
source: It is possible that this trade-off is shifted toward the stable side in Disc1-mutant mice
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional consequences in Disc1-mutant mice.

claim: A shift toward stable representation might possibly hinder the flexible allocation of new compared to previously encoded memory contents.
source: which might possibly hinder the flexible allocation of new compared to previously encoded memory contents.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cognitive consequences.

claim: mPFC-dependent working memory requires dynamic updating of memory.
source: Since mPFC-dependent working memory requires dynamic updating of memory
evidence: This is established knowledge about working memory function.

claim: A shift toward stable representation might contribute to impaired working memory performance of Disc1-mutant mice.
source: a shift toward stable representation might contribute to impaired working memory performance of Disc1-mutant mice (Kvajo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of working memory impairment, with citation to behavioral study.
